This bill would tighten rules on travel benefits for current and former parliamentarians.
It would add a 25% penalty on incorrect travel claims and limit children's travel to those under 18.
The Life Gold Pass scheme would be renamed the Parliamentary Retirement Travel Entitlement, with benefits reduced or removed for most former members except former prime ministers.
Adds a 25% loading to certain travel claim adjustments.
Reduces the age limit for children's travel from 25 to 18.
Renames the Life Gold Pass scheme and cuts benefits.
Imposes expiry dates on travel entitlements.
Closes the scheme to new retirees after the bill starts.
Removes spouse travel except for former prime ministers.
Current and former parliamentarians, their spouses and children, and the Department of Finance.

The bill terminates Life Gold Pass travel for all current holders except retired former prime ministers and their spouses, renames the remaining benefit to parliamentary retirement travel, removes spousal travel for other former parliamentarians, reduces travel for former prime ministers, imposes a 25 per cent penalty on adjusted travel claims unless corrected within 28 days, and establishes a constitutional mechanism for recovering overpayments.

The opposition supported the Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 to remove the Life Gold Pass from all current and future recipients, arguing the entitlement is inappropriate amid high economic insecurity and no longer meets community standards.

The speaker opposed the Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, arguing that retrospectively abolishing the Life Gold Pass from 14 May 2014 for long-serving former MPs—who earned it over 21 years under different salary conditions—was a dangerous precedent, while supporting other provisions like a 25% loading for deliberate travel claim misrepresentations and limiting dependent children’s travel to under 18.

The speaker argued the Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill is "too little, too late" and a kneejerk reaction, criticising the 25 per cent penalty loading on incorrect claims as insufficient while supporting the end of the Life Gold Pass for former MPs except Prime Ministers. They foreshadowed an amendment to substantially increase penalties and estimated that requiring economy class for flights under two hours would save over $2 million annually.

The Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 accelerates the end of the Life Gold Pass travel scheme for all current holders except retired former prime ministers and their spouses, limits former prime ministers to 30 domestic return trips per year and their spouses to 20, and reduces the dependent child travel age from under-25 to under-18. The bill also introduces a 25% penalty loading on claims requiring adjustment unless due to departmental error or corrected within 28 days, and creates a mechanism to recover payments beyond entitlement.

The Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 was supported, which establishes an independent authority (modelled on the UK IPSA) to administer claims and provide monthly public disclosure of MPs' and senators' expenses. An amendment will be moved to add a community representative to the authority's board, which currently comprises the President of the Remuneration Tribunal, a former MP, a former judiciary member, and an auditor.
